frames.narration: One job arrives every tick. A pool of 4 worker threads takes jobs from a queue. A job here is 2 ticks of CPU and then 10 ticks of waiting for I/O, so it holds its thread for 12 ticks.
4 threads can finish only 1 job every 3 ticks, but jobs arrive every tick. The queue grows by 2 jobs every 3 ticks: 40 waiting by the end, and each job spends 68 ticks in the system on average.
Little's law gives the size: 1 job per tick times 12 ticks in the system is 12 threads. With 12 threads the queue stays empty and a job takes 12 ticks, the time it really needs.

Now CPU-bound jobs of 8 ticks each. Only 4 threads can compute at once, so 4 threads already use every core. 64 threads finish no sooner; they just hold 49 half-finished jobs and make the average job slower.
What sits in front of the pool matters under overload. An unbounded queue accepts everything, and waiting time grows. A queue bounded to 10 rejects jobs at once, and the accepted ones wait less.

The trap: each job submits a sub-job to the same pool and waits for it. With 4 threads, all 4 fill up with waiting parents. The sub-jobs sit in the queue behind them and the pool deadlocks, with no error.
Fix it with a separate pool for sub-jobs, or by not blocking while waiting, or with a pool big enough for the parents plus the sub-jobs. With 12 threads the same load finishes in 40 ticks.
